chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, all together from Ibn Mahbub, from Abu Hamza al-Thumali, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

There used to be among the Children of Israel a judge who used to judge with the truth among them. When death came to him, he said to his wife: 'When I die, wash me, shroud me, place me on my bed, and cover my face — for you will not see evil.'

When he died, she did that and remained thus for a while. Then she uncovered his face in order to look at him, and behold there was a worm gnawing at his nostril! She was terrified by that. When night came, he appeared to her in her dream and said to her: 'Did what you saw terrify you?' She said: 'Yes, I was indeed terrified.'

So he said to her: 'Know that if you were frightened, that which you saw was nothing but because of your brother, so-and-so. He came to me with an adversary of his. When they both sat before me, I said: O Allah, make the right be for him and direct the judgment against his companion! When they disputed before me, the right was indeed with him and I saw that clearly in the case — so I directed the judgment in his favor against his companion. Thus what you saw struck me, because of where my desire was — even though it was in agreement with the truth.'

key_terms.الْحَقِّ: haqq — truth, right, justice; that which conforms to divine law
key_terms.الْقَضَاءُ: al-qada — the act of judicial judgment, the ruling itself
key_terms.بَنُو إِسْرَائِيلَ: Banu Isra'il — the Children of Israel; in Shia hadith, often used as a paradigmatic community for moral instruction
key_terms.قاضٍ: a judge (qadi) — one appointed to adjudicate legal disputes according to Islamic law
key_terms.هَوَى: hawa — personal desire, whim, inclination; in jurisprudence, the internal bias that corrupts judgment

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on a judge who correctly decides a case but with prior personal bias?
ai.summary: This hadith narrates a cautionary tale about a righteous judge from the Children of Israel who, despite rendering a correct verdict, secretly harbored a predetermined desire for one party to win before hearing the case. Though the outcome was just, his internal bias — his hawa (whim/desire) — was punished posthumously. The story illustrates the Shia jurisprudential principle that a judge must approach every case with complete impartiality, and that even an outwardly correct ruling is corrupted by secret partiality. The original audience — students of jurisprudence in early Islamic society — would have understood this as a stern warning that divine accountability penetrates even the hidden intentions of judges.

en.hubeali:
A number of our companions, from Sahl Bin Ziyad and Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, both together from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Hamza Al Sumaly, 
Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> has said:

‘There used to be among the Children of Israel, a judge who used to judge with the truth. So when the death presented itself, he said to his wife, ‘When I die, so wash me and shroud me, and place me upon my bed and cover up my face, so that you cannot see evil’.

So when he died, she did that. Then she remained with that for a while, then she uncovered from his face in order to look at him. So there was an insect in his nostril. So she panicked from that. So when it was the night, he came in her dream, so he said to her, ‘What did you see (which) terrified you?’ She said, ‘Yes, I had panicked’.

So he said to her, ‘That which you panicked from what you saw was nothing except with regards to your brother. So and so came to me and with him was an adversary of his. So when they were seated to me, I said, ‘O Allah<sup>azwj</sup>! Make the truth be for him and the aspect of the judgement to be against his companion’. 
So when they had disputed to me, and the truth was for him, and I saw that proof in the judgement, so I turned the judgement for him against his companion. Thus, what you saw, hit me, for the placing of my whim although it was in accordance with the truth’.
en.sarwar: 2. A number of our people have narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad and Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from all from ibn Mahbub from abu Hamzah al-Thumaliy who has narrated the following: “Abu Ja‘far, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said

among the Israelites there was a judge who judged with the truth. When his death approached, he said to his woman, ‘When I die, wash my body, shroud me, place me on my bed and cover my head so you do not see anything bad.’

When he died, she followed his instructions and waited for some time; then she opened his face to look at him and found a worm cutting his nostril. She was shocked because of it and at night he came in her dream and asked, ‘Did what you saw shock you?’ She replied, ‘Yes, it shocked me.’

He said, ‘That was because of your brother who had a dispute with another man and they came to me for judgment. Only in my heart, I said, ‘O Lord, make the right to be on his side.’ When they presented their case, the right was on the side of your brother, which I saw clearly in the rules of judgment. Just for what I said in my heart I face the suffering that shocked you even though it was in accordance with the truth.’”
